title: Woven rib lap throw
subtitle: A 100 by 120 cm lap throw in woven rib stitch on 5 mm needles, DK.
excerpt: A 100 by 120 cm lap throw worked flat in woven rib (also called tweed stitch) on 5 mm needles. The slip-stitch woven structure gives the fabric a tweed-like texture and excellent drape without any colour-changing. About 800 g of DK.
sourceNotes: Weldon's Practical Knitter, 11th series (1895), §Woven Stitch, describes the slip-stitch woven texture as a drawing-room throw pattern. Barbara Walker, A Treasury of Knitting Patterns (1968), §Woven Patterns, documents the four-row slip sequence under the name Tweed Stitch.

knitting.gaugeText: 20 sts × 30 rows = 10 × 10 cm in woven rib on 5 mm needles. Woven rib draws in slightly compared to stocking stitch on the same needle.

glossaryTerms.definition: A slip-stitch texture pattern that uses a four-row repeat to create interlocking horizontal floats on the wrong side and a tweedy surface on the right side. Only knit and purl actions are used on right-side rows; wrong-side rows slip alternate stitches to create the woven-looking floats. Single colour only; no stranding required.

content.text: A single-panel rectangle worked flat on 5 mm needles in
woven rib stitch
, finishing at 100 cm wide by 120 cm long.

Single-panel construction; no seaming. Woven rib was chosen because the slip-stitch structure creates a denser fabric than stocking stitch on the same needle size, giving a throw-weight warmth from DK yarn. Only one colour is used; the texture comes from the slip pattern, not from colour changes. The larger 5 mm needle ensures the fabric does not become stiff. Budget about 800 g (about 1,760 m / 1,920 yards) of DK. Buy in matched dye lots.
What you need

items.name: Yarn
items.qty: 800 g (about 1,760 m / 1,920 yards) of DK-weight yarn. A smooth single-colour DK shows the texture clearly.

items.name: Needles
items.qty: 5 mm (UK 6 / US 8) circular needle, 120 cm or longer

content.text: Gauge
20 stitches and 30 rows to 10 cm in woven rib on 5 mm needles, unblocked. Swatch the full 4-row repeat for at least 12 cm; woven rib draws in more than stocking stitch at this needle size.
If your stitch gauge is 18 per 10 cm with 200 stitches, the throw will be about 111 cm wide. Adjust the cast-on in multiples of 4 to match a 100 cm target.
Stitches used
Pattern
Cast-on
Using the long-tail cast-on, cast on 200 stitches (a multiple of 4). Long-tail tail: (5 × 200) / 10 + 15 = 100 + 15 = 115 cm. Measure 130 cm.
Body (4-row repeat)
Row 1 (RS): *k1, sl1wyb; repeat from * to end.
Row 2 (WS): *p1, sl1wyf; repeat from * to end.
Row 3 (RS): *sl1wyb, k1; repeat from * to end.
Row 4 (WS): *sl1wyf, p1; repeat from * to end.
Repeat rows 1 to 4 until the throw measures 120 cm. When you set this aside, note which of the four rows is next.
Stitch count check-ins
At row 180 (about 60 cm): count across. You should have 200 stitches. Woven rib never changes stitch count. At row 358 (about 119 cm): count again before casting off.
Common faults

Woven surface appearing as plain stocking stitch: the slip offset was the same on rows 1 and 3 rather than alternating. Row 1 slips on even-position stitches; row 3 slips on odd-position stitches, the slip must shift by one stitch between these rows.
Floats showing on the right side: yarn was kept in front on a RS slipped stitch instead of behind. On RS rows, yarn always goes to the back before slipping.
Cast-off
Cast off knitwise with a relaxed tension at the end of row 4 of a complete repeat.
Finishing
Weave in ends. The woven rib fabric lies flat without blocking. A gentle wash will even out the slip-stitch texture.
Care
Machine wash on a gentle 30-degree cycle for superwash DK. Lay flat to dry.
What to try next

From single-colour woven rib, try a two-colour version where the slip stitches are in a contrast colour: alternate 2 rows of colour A (knit/purl) with 2 rows of colour B (all slipped on the alternating positions). The result is a more pronounced textured surface.
